concept.technique_name: Sesani Ankena Caramena (multiply each remainder by the last digit of the divisor)

examples.problem_statement: ⅐ The remainders are 3, 2, 6, 4, 5 and 1.

solution.description: The problem hands you the six remainders 3, 2, 6, 4, 5 and 1 left by dividing 1 by 7. Recognise that these six remainders are exactly what generate the six repeating decimal places of one seventh, so the whole expansion can be read off them without further long division.

solution.operation: Apply Nikhilam Sutra: All from 9, last from 10
solution.description: Fix the working rule that will be used on every remainder: the Caramanka is the last digit of the divisor, which for 7 is 7 itself. Multiply a remainder by that Caramanka and keep only the units digit of the product; that units digit is the quotient digit for the matching decimal place.
Take the first remainder, 3. Three times seven is twenty one, and keeping only the units digit gives 1, so the first decimal place of one seventh is 1.
Move to the second remainder, 2. Two times seven is fourteen, whose units digit is 4, so the second decimal place is 4.
Move to the third remainder, 6. Six times seven is forty two, whose units digit is 2, so the third decimal place is 2.
Move to the fourth remainder, 4. Four times seven is twenty eight, whose units digit is 8, so the fourth decimal place is 8.
Move to the fifth remainder, 5. Five times seven is thirty five, whose units digit is 5, so the fifth decimal place is 5.
Move to the last remainder, 1. One times seven is seven, and its units digit is 7, giving the sixth decimal place.
Read the six quotient digits back in the order their remainders were used: 1, 4, 2, 8, 5, 7. Because the remainders then repeat, this block repeats forever, so one seventh is 0.142857 recurring.

solution.operation: Multiply each remainder by 3 (the last digit): 10×3=30, 9×3=27, 12×3=36, 3×3=9, 4×3=12, 1×3=3.
solution.description: Here the divisor is 13, so the Caramanka is its last digit, 3. Multiply each given remainder by 3 in the order listed: 10 gives 30, 9 gives 27, 12 gives 36, 3 gives 9, 4 gives 12 and 1 gives 3. Nothing else about 13 is needed.

solution.operation: Write down only the last digit of each product: 0, 7, 6, 9, 2, 3.
solution.description: Discard the tens of every product and keep only the units digit, which leaves 0, 7, 6, 9, 2 and 3. Read in the same order these are the successive decimal places, so one thirteenth is 0.076923 recurring.
The divisor is 17, so the Caramanka is its last digit, 7. Multiply every remainder in the given list by 7, keeping the remainders strictly in the order the division produced them.

solution.operation: Take the last digit of each product to form the quotient digits.
solution.description: Take only the last digit of each of those products. Read in the same order, those digits are the successive decimal places of one seventeenth, one digit per remainder.

concept.technique_name: Geometrical progression of remainders (advance by the ratio 3, casting out sevens)

examples.problem_statement: Find the decimal expansion of \frac{1}{7} using the Geometrical Progression of remainders.

solution.description: Dividing 1 by 7 in decimal form leaves 3 as the first remainder, so the chain starts there. Every later remainder in this example is built from this one.

The remainders of one seventh advance by a constant ratio of 3. Multiply the current remainder 3 by 3 to get 9; since 9 exceeds the divisor, cast out one seven, and 9 minus 7 leaves 2 as the second remainder.
Apply the same ratio to 2: two times three is six. That is already smaller than 7, so nothing is cast out and 6 stands as the third remainder.
Multiply 6 by the ratio 3 to get 18. Two sevens fit inside 18, so cast out 14 rather than 7, and 18 minus 14 leaves 4 as the fourth remainder.
Multiply 4 by the ratio 3 to get 12. One seven comes out, and 12 minus 7 leaves 5 as the fifth remainder.
Multiply 5 by the ratio 3 to get 15. Two sevens come out, and 15 minus 14 leaves 1 as the sixth remainder. Reaching 1 signals that the cycle is complete.
Collect the chain in the order it was built: 3, 2, 6, 4, 5, 1. These six remainders are the whole repeating cycle for one seventh, and no seventh remainder is needed.

solution.operation: Multiply each remainder by Caramāṅka (7) and take the rightmost digit to get quotient digits: ·1, 4, 2, 8, 5, 7.
solution.description: Convert the remainders into decimal places by multiplying each one by the Caramanka 7, the last digit of the divisor, and keeping only the units digit of each product. The six remainders yield the digits 1, 4, 2, 8, 5 and 7.

solution.operation: Apply the D ~ N rule: since 6 is the complement of the numerator (1) relative to the denominator (7), stop and find the remaining remainders by complements.

If you would rather keep computing than use the complement shortcut, carry on with the ratio 3: six times three is eighteen, less fourteen leaves 4; four times three is twelve, less seven leaves 5; five times three is fifteen, less fourteen leaves 1. Both routes give the same chain.

solution.description: Close the example the same way as before: multiply each remainder by the Caramanka 7 and keep only the last digit of each product, which gives the quotient digits 1, 4, 2, 8, 5 and 7.

examples.problem_statement: Using the Vedic Mathematics technique for finding decimal expansion of fractions, demonstrate how to find the decimal expansion of $\frac{1}{7}$ using the concept of remainders and Carmāṅkas (right-hand-most digits). Given that the first remainder is 3, show how to find all subsequent remainders and the corresponding quotient digits.

solution.operation: Multiply each remainder by 3 and subtract multiples of 7 to get next remainder:
Multiply each remainder by 7 to get quotient digits:
Identify the first remainder for $\frac{1}{7}$, which is 3.
Multiply the first remainder by 3 (the Geometrical ratio): $3 \times 3 = 9$. Cast out sevens: $9 - 7 = 2$. The second remainder is 2.
Multiply the second remainder by 3: $2 \times 3 = 6$. The third remainder is 6.
Multiply the third remainder by 3: $6 \times 3 = 18$. Cast out sevens: $18 - 14 = 4$. The fourth remainder is 4.
Multiply the fourth remainder by 3: $4 \times 3 = 12$. Cast out sevens: $12 - 7 = 5$. The fifth remainder is 5.
Multiply the fifth remainder by 3: $5 \times 3 = 15$. Cast out sevens: $15 - 14 = 1$. The sixth (and last) remainder is 1.
The complete sequence of remainders is 3, 2, 6, 4, 5, 1.

Multiply each remainder by the Caramāṅka (7) to get the quotient-digits: $3 \times 7 = 21$ (digit 1), $2 \times 7 = 14$ (digit 4), $6 \times 7 = 42$ (digit 2), $4 \times 7 = 28$ (digit 8), $5 \times 7 = 35$ (digit 5), $1 \times 7 = 7$ (digit 7).
The quotient digits are 1, 4, 2, 8, 5, 7, giving the decimal expansion $\frac{1}{7} = 0.\dot{1}4285\dot{7}$.

concept.technique_name: Successive remainders in the decimal expansion of a reciprocal (divide, record the digit, carry the remainder)

examples.problem_statement: Find the decimal expansion of $\frac{1}{17}$ using the method of remainders and Caramāṅkas (units digits). The problem demonstrates how to find the complete set of remainders when dividing 1 by 17, and then multiplying each remainder's units digit by 7 to obtain the decimal digits.

solution.description: One is smaller than 17, so the units place of the quotient is 0 and the whole 1 stays behind as remainder. Bring down a zero to make 10, the working remainder that opens the decimal places.
Carry the remainder 10 into the next place: attach a zero to make 100, divide by 17 to get 5, and 15 is left over. So the first decimal digit is 5 and 15 becomes the remainder for the next step.
Carry the remainder 15 into the next place: attach a zero to make 150, divide by 17 to get 8, and 14 is left over. So the second decimal digit is 8 and 14 becomes the remainder for the next step.
Carry the remainder 14 into the next place: attach a zero to make 140, divide by 17 to get 8, and 4 is left over. So the third decimal digit is 8 and 4 becomes the remainder for the next step.
Carry the remainder 4 into the next place: attach a zero to make 40, divide by 17 to get 2, and 6 is left over. So the fourth decimal digit is 2 and 6 becomes the remainder for the next step.
Carry the remainder 6 into the next place: attach a zero to make 60, divide by 17 to get 3, and 9 is left over. So the fifth decimal digit is 3 and 9 becomes the remainder for the next step.
Carry the remainder 9 into the next place: attach a zero to make 90, divide by 17 to get 5, and 5 is left over. So the sixth decimal digit is 5 and 5 becomes the remainder for the next step.
Carry the remainder 5 into the next place: attach a zero to make 50, divide by 17 to get 2, and 16 is left over. So the seventh decimal digit is 2 and 16 becomes the remainder for the next step.
Carry the remainder 16 into the next place: attach a zero to make 160, divide by 17 to get 9, and 7 is left over. So the eighth decimal digit is 9 and 7 becomes the remainder for the next step.
Carry the remainder 7 into the next place: attach a zero to make 70, divide by 17 to get 4, and 2 is left over. So the ninth decimal digit is 4 and 2 becomes the remainder for the next step.
Carry the remainder 2 into the next place: attach a zero to make 20, divide by 17 to get 1, and 3 is left over. So the tenth decimal digit is 1 and 3 becomes the remainder for the next step.
Carry the remainder 3 into the next place: attach a zero to make 30, divide by 17 to get 1, and 13 is left over. So the eleventh decimal digit is 1 and 13 becomes the remainder for the next step.
Carry the remainder 13 into the next place: attach a zero to make 130, divide by 17 to get 7, and 11 is left over. So the twelfth decimal digit is 7 and 11 becomes the remainder for the next step.
Carry the remainder 11 into the next place: attach a zero to make 110, divide by 17 to get 6, and 8 is left over. So the thirteenth decimal digit is 6 and 8 becomes the remainder for the next step.
Carry the remainder 8 into the next place: attach a zero to make 80, divide by 17 to get 4, and 12 is left over. So the fourteenth decimal digit is 4 and 12 becomes the remainder for the next step.
Carry the remainder 12 into the next place: attach a zero to make 120, divide by 17 to get 7, and 1 is left over. So the fifteenth decimal digit is 7 and 1 becomes the remainder for the next step.

Carry the remainder 1 forward one more time: attach a zero to make 10, and 17 does not go into 10, so the digit is 0 and the remainder is 10 again. That 10 is the remainder the expansion started with, which proves the cycle has closed.

String the digits together in the order they were produced, starting with the leading zero: 0588235294117647. Because the remainder 10 has returned, this block of sixteen digits repeats without end, giving the full expansion of one seventeenth.

examples.problem_statement: Convert the fraction $\frac{1}{19}$ to a recurring decimal using the Ekādhika method. Show how this method simplifies the division process by using the Ekādhika-pūrva (2 for 19) instead of dividing by 19 directly.

solution.description: The Ekadhika is one more than the previous digit. For 19, the previous digit is 1, so Ekadhika = 2.
We begin the process from the rightmost digit of the decimal expansion. Start with 1 (numerator) as the last digit
Multiply the current digit (1) by Ekadhika (2). Write down 2 as the next digit to the left. (no carry)
Multiply the new digit (2) by Ekadhika (2). Write down 4 as the next digit to the left. (no carry)
Multiply the new digit (4) by Ekadhika (2). Write down 8 as the next digit to the left. (no carry)
Multiply 8 by 2 to get 16. Write down 6 and carry over 1 to the next step. (write 6, carry 1)
Multiply 6 by 2 and add the carried 1 to get 13. Write down 3 and carry 1. (write 3, carry 1)
Multiply 3 by 2 and add the carried 1 to get 7. Write down 7. (no carry)
Multiply 7 by 2 to get 14. Write down 4 and carry 1. (write 4, carry 1)
Multiply 4 by 2 and add the carried 1 to get 9. Write down 9. (no carry)
Multiply 9 by 2 to get 18. Write down 8 and carry 1. (write 8, carry 1)
Multiply 8 by 2 and add the carried 1 to get 17. Write down 7 and carry 1. (write 7, carry 1)
Multiply 7 by 2 and add the carried 1 to get 15. Write down 5 and carry 1. (write 5, carry 1)

Multiply 1 by 2 and add the carried 1 to get 3. Write down 3. (no carry)
Multiply 3 by 2 to get 6. Write down 6. (no carry)

concept.technique_name: Turning the denominator into a string of nines using the identity 73 times 137 equals 10001
concept.sub_category: Ekadhikena Purvena (One More than the Previous)

examples.problem_statement: $\frac{1}{73}$ is special. Since $73 \times 137 = 10001$ and since $10001 \times 9999 = 99999999$

solution.description: We use the property that 73 times 137 = 10001, which is a number of the form 10^n + 1

solution.operation: Express fraction using the special property
solution.description: Multiply numerator and denominator by 137 to utilize the special property
We multiply by 9999 to get a denominator of 99999999, which will help in decimal conversion
Using the Vedic Math sutra 'Nikhilam Navatashcaramam Dashatah' (all from 9 and last from 10) for multiplication by 9999
When dividing by 99,999,999, the numerator becomes the repeating decimal block
The decimal repeats every 8 digits: 01369863

examples.problem_statement: Conversely, $\frac{1}{137}$

solution.description: Turn the identity around for the reciprocal of the other factor. Since 73 times 137 is 10001, multiplying the top and bottom of one over 137 by 73 replaces the denominator with 10001 and leaves 73 on top.

Multiply top and bottom by 9999 so the denominator becomes 10001 times 9999, that is 99999999, a string of eight nines. Over a denominator of all nines the numerator itself becomes the repeating block.

Work out the new numerator as 73 times 10000 less 73, which is 730000 minus 73, or 729927. Padded with a leading zero to fill the eight places demanded by the eight nines, the recurring block is 00729927, so one over 137 is 0.00729927 recurring.

solution.description: We are finding the decimal expansion of 1/41. The divisor is 41, which is a prime number.

We rewrite 41 as 40 + 1 to apply the sutra. This allows us to use the geometric series expansion.

solution.description: For |x| < 1, we can expand 1/(1+x) as an alternating geometric series.
Substitute x = 1/40 into the series expansion.
Calculate the first few terms to see the pattern.

Multiplying the result by 41 should give us 1, confirming our decimal expansion is correct.

examples.problem_statement: Find the decimal expansion of 1/13 using Ekādhika Pūrva methods.

solution.description: The Ekādhika is one more than the previous digit. For 13, we take the last digit 3, add 1 to get 4. This will be our multiplier.
We know 1/13 is a repeating decimal with period 6. We'll use the Ekādhika method to generate the digits.
Start with 1 (numerator). Multiply by Ekādhika (4). Since 4 < 10, we write 0 and carry 4.
Take the carry (4), multiply by Ekādhika (4) to get 16. Write 6, carry 1.
Take the carry (1), multiply by Ekādhika (4) to get 4. Write 4, no carry.
Take the current digit (4), multiply by Ekādhika (4) to get 16. Write 6, carry 1.
Take the carry (1), multiply by Ekādhika (4) to get 4. Write 4, no carry.
Take the current digit (4), multiply by Ekādhika (4) to get 16. Write 6, carry 1.
The pattern repeats every 6 digits. We can verify: 1/13 = 0.076923076923...
